chapter_theme: The ninth ten, Perunkunrur Kizhar's songs for Ilanjeral Irumporai: the king's camp in the rains and a plea to go home to the queen so the besieged may sleep, the inexhaustible wealth and army, a march sweet to watch and bitter to meet, foes who knew his strength and would not bow, gifts beyond Kapilar's villages, a fierce king gentler than the Vaani's water, a singer sent for jewels, the ancestors' deeds against Nannan and the kadamba, rain brought by a straight sceptre, and a king likened to water, sky and sea; the preface adds his Chola wars and his rites.

new_concepts.gloss: the war camp of a king in the field, where the army stays through a campaign
new_concepts.label_source: the text names it: பாசறை யோர்க்கே (83 line 9), பார்வல் பாசறை (84 line 5), வெல்கொடி நுடங்கும் பாசறை (88 line 17)

81.reading: When the rain cloud, fierce and heavy with water, thunders across the sky at morning and brings loneliness, the poet describes the king's camp in a foreign land, where elephants charge, horses are reined, chariots wheel, and warriors who keep their bracelets bright even in the dark night and make long vows to fix their clan's fame circle the wide rock floor, while in Kolli the rich hill folk with kaanthal garlands drink sweet toddy matured in bamboo and give to suppliants; then he asks the king to yoke his horses to his tall chariot for one day to see his jewelled wife with soft words and loving eyes, so that the enemy kings who keep to their forts sleepless, afraid their old line will be cut off, may sleep too, and her embrace be a feast for his great shoulders.
81.nuance: The return home is asked for as a mercy to the enemy as well as a joy for the king: the last three lines make the besieged kings' sleep depend on the queen's embrace. The opening cloud is the rainy season of mullai, when the absent man is due home, so the bard uses the akam occasion to end a war poem.

thinai_evidence.note: the poet asks the king to leave the camp in the rainy season to see his wife

comparisons.tenor: the rainy-season abundance of the hill folk
the bright jewels of the wife's companions

thurai_akam.speaker: pira
thurai_akam.note: the poet, a bard, speaks to the king as husband

82.reading: The poet says he came to see and sing the king's long stay in the dreadful camp, which fears no hard toll, whose many flags wave, where the war elephant that destroyed the foes' battles walks with its bee-haunted mate, musth flowing, where warriors clash, cavalry strikes, chariot flags wave and shields resound, a camp that has scorched the forest, with many days such as this; and he praises the tall king who has wealth given by the land, which never lessens however much singers take, an army that never lessens however much foes kill, and generosity, rectitude, nobility and valour of an unshaken fame.
82.nuance: The closing pair is built as one formula (கொளக்கொளக் குறையா / கொலக்கொலக் குறையா): the same endless supply serves the singers who take and the army the foes cut down, so giving and fighting are measured alike. The first line has the god speak because the enmity is great, a hint that the war began with an omen.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem describes the king's long encampment in the land he invaded

83.reading: The poet tells the king that his advance, with elephants massed among many shields and tall chariots whose waving flags shine, splendid as the long line of high-flying cranes that rises before the rain clouds, is very sweet to those who watch it, but bitter indeed to the kings in the rival camp who must face his fierce rage, which ruins lands of many horses and brings back fine jewels.
83.nuance: One sight is given two audiences: the onlookers for whom the march is beautiful and the enemy camp for whom it is ruin, and the poem turns on the pair இனிது and இன்னாது.

thinai_evidence.note: the army marches to meet the rival kings in battle

comparisons.tenor: the long line of the army with elephants, shields and chariots

84.reading: The poet hails the lord of the Puzhiyar, Poraiyan of the golden chariot, mighty as Death who crushes mankind, whose trained war elephant, when the rain cloud roars like the struck war drum, slips its tether and rises with lifted brow; though his foes knew well that he was strong, they did not count his countless flag-topped forts and his land of horses as one, and like forked bamboo shoots trampled by a young elephant maddened by the thunder, those who provoked him could not escape: not knowing how to bow, they rose together with drums sounding, and in the spear-crowded field elephants fell like thunder-struck hills; having fought many battles worthy of kaanchi, he sits in a crowded camp the poet has gladly seen, loud as the many-voiced birds when the morning rain has done its work on the hills.
84.nuance: The foes are not ignorant: line 10 says they knew his strength well, and line 14 that they did not know how to bow, so their ruin comes from pride rather than from a mistake. The poem opens and closes on rain, with the elephant roused by thunder and the camp loud as birds after rain.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem celebrates the king's victories over those who rose against him

comparisons.tenor: the roar of the rain cloud

comparisons.vehicle: மழகளிறு மிகீஇத்தன் கால்முளை மூங்கில் கவர்கிளை போல
comparisons.tenor: the foes who provoked the king
elephants falling to the ground in battle
the clamour of the king's crowded camp

85.reading: The poet says that what the king gives, he who trampled many lands thick with good trees and made the hostile lord of the Chenniyar, of gleaming gold ornament, yield white pearls, and who stands like the founders of his ancient line in the daily revel on the long land-viewing hill with its many peaks and sweet springs, is more than the villages won by Kapilan, the poet of good fame and shining red tongue, of valiant creed and a heart without care, who sang before a royal assembly that bowed to him.
85.nuance: The measure of the king's giving is another poet's reward: Kapilar, who sang the king's grandfather in the seventh ten, is named so that this ten's gifts can be said to exceed his. சூடா நறவின் (line 8) and the half-line about the Chola's spear and pearls (line 4) are hard to construe; the subject of the final பலவே is left to be supplied.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem praises the king's giving by setting it above a famous earlier reward

86.reading: The poet says that when he heard men call him Poraiyan of the victorious spear, whose fierce strong hand killed and won in war and made the blood-soaked field stink, he feared him as a man of heat; but this lord of swaying gait, patron of singers, with a kind heart worth seeking, who gives to end the misery of the poor in the wide world where good fame stays, is surely sweeter and cooler of gentleness than the water of the Vaani, which brings down sandal and in whose pools, too deep for a bamboo pole to touch bottom, the gold flower earrings lost by bathing women show on the surface.
86.nuance: The poem is built as a correction: the report of slaughter (lines 1 to 3) made the poet afraid, and the meeting shows the opposite temper. The river image keeps both: the pools are too deep to fathom, yet the water is cool and clear enough to show the lost earrings.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem praises the king's kindness to singers and the poor

87.reading: The poet tells a singing woman to go, for she will receive fine jewels: Poraiyan of many spears is more given to kindness than the sugarcane carried along the water's course of the red flood, white-crested with swelling foam, that bears sandal and akil down to the clear sea.
87.nuance: The whole guide poem is five lines: the road, the patron and the gifts of the longer guide poems are compressed into one image of a river carrying fragrant wood to the sea, which already pictures wealth flowing outward. Whether the cane is sweet or yielding (bending with the flow) is not settled by the line.

thinai_evidence.note: the poet sends a singer to the king for gifts

88.reading: The poet hails the descendant of the great ones who, never abandoning the order that made the world flourish, hurled a spear so that the dark sea of a hostile country was destroyed, cut down the whole trunk of the spirit-guarded kadamba, saw the back of Kazhuvul, crushed famed kings, drove off the Andar of swift horses, wore down Nannan of the bright-flowered vaakai and worshipped Ayirai with heaps of blood-sprinkled rice, so that kings and Velir followed and bowed; he calls him lion-maned chief, king of the Kongar, lord of the people of Tondi whose drum is the curving sea, whose camp has banners on strong elephants and slings that batter forts, whose gifts flow to all comers without restraint like a great river in flood and never lessen however taken, who in a mansion like a painting among women like dolls wears sandal and garlands on a chest like a hill with waterfalls where vengai blooms and clouds gather, husband of a jewelled lady of far-spread fame; may he live long and shine like the sun, lord of the cool sea-shore land where wind-raised waves break on fine sand, for the poet has come to see him.
88.nuance: The deeds in lines 4 to 13 are the ancestors' (பெரியோர் மருக, line 14), not the present king's: the sea-spear and the kadamba of the second ten and Nannan's vaakai of the fourth are gathered into one inherited record. Lines 23 and 24 (துவைத்த தும்பை நனவுற்று வினவும்) are obscure.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem praises the king's line and blesses him

comparisons.tenor: the many gifts that flow to all comers
the king's chest with sandal and garlands
the roar of the sea at Tondi

89.reading: The poet says that because Irumporai's sceptre is straight, the sky pours in its season, in the forest the young doe of the herd walks with its stag, birds and bees hum on the dark boughs, fruit and tubers never fail, fine herds of cattle graze and frisk, grain abounds with a yield that knows no end and justice holds for many ages, so that the land worships him day by day and those of the high world praise him; never erring in kingship and great in war, may he be free of illness together with his bright-browed wife, whose heart, bound to him, knows no fault, who never parts from him even in dreams, whose hair is smoothed with tagaram, and whose chastity is like the star that brides look at in the wedding rite.
89.nuance: The plenty of lines 1 to 8 is the effect of a cause stated only in line 9 (நின்கோல் செம்மையின்), so the land's order is read back from the king's justice. The doe walking with its stag (line 2) is the forest's picture of the union the poem then blesses in the queen; in a puram poem it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem praises the king's just rule and blesses him and his wife

90.reading: The poet hails the descendant of victorious Mantharan, who ruled so well that dharma praised him, while the stars kept their places, the sky gave rain, fear and darkness left, joy grew and kings with gleaming swords brought him elephants and jewels and heard his commands; he tells the king that he is like water for his kindness, like the sky for being beyond measure, like the sea for not lessening however taken, that he shines among his flowering kin like the moon among many stars, and heir of mighty ones who worshipped Ayirai, made the sea retreat with a spear, broke the strength of foes and seized the forts of hill and plain; he names him king of the Kongar, bull of the Kuttuvar, shield of the Puzhiyar, lord of the people of Maranthai and king of the warriors of a camp of mixed tongues, who with an army like the sea draws his great bow to his chest, rides a plumed horse with gem trappings bright as blossoming stars and hurls the lance, chief of warriors of unretreating courage, husband of a bright-bangled lady of calm chastity as rich as the good Kaveri land where field peacocks dance to the ploughmen's drum taking it for rain; and he says he came to see him wishing that his days be as months, months as years, years as ages and ages beyond count, lord of great elephants and of drums that roar like thunder.
90.nuance: Each of the three likenesses in lines 14 to 16 names its own ground (ஈரம், அளப்பருமை, கொளக்குறைபடாமை), so the poem does the work of saying what water, sky and sea share with the king. The closing wish multiplies time step by step, days to months to years to ages to a countless number. The peacock that mistakes the field drum for thunder (line 42) is a picture of plenty, not a comparison with the king.

thinai_evidence.note: the poet praises the king's line, titles and deeds and blesses his life

comparisons.tenor: the king's wealth that does not lessen when taken
the gem trappings of the horse
the abundance of the king's wife

patikam:9.reading: The decade's preface says that Ilanjeral Irumporai, son of Kuttuvan Irumporai by Velmal Anthuvan Chellai, daughter of the lord of Maiyur, made war hot with a dreadful army so that the two great kings and Vichchi fell, razed five forts in the stony land of hard thickets, defeated Perunchozhan who ruled Poththi and Ilampazhaiyan Maran who ruled Viththai as his vow had said, brought the spoils to the old town of Vanji and helped others with them, tended the god in the way of the mantras, set the truthful minister, the lord of Maiyur, beside the purohita of faultless learning, brought the fierce spirits of the great crossroads and installed them here, performed the rite of peace and guarded living beings with a flawless sceptre; Perunkunrur Kizhar sang this ten.
patikam:9.nuance: Half the preface is ritual, not war: mantra worship, the purohita, the installed spirits and the shanti rite follow the victories, as if the preface-writer counted these among a Chera king's deeds. Lines 11 and 12 (மெய்யூர் அமைச்சியன் ... புரோசு மயக்கி) are hard to construe.

thinai_evidence.note: the preface praises the king's victories, rites and just rule

links.note: Akananuru 44 has a man bid his charioteer hurry home to his wife because the king's war is finished and the foes have paid tribute; Patitruppattu 81 has the poet ask the king himself, in the rainy season with the siege still on, to yoke his chariot for one day to see his wife, so that the sleepless besieged kings may sleep too (துஞ்சா வேந்தரும் துஞ்சுக).
links.teaches: In the akam poem the homecoming waits until the war is over, but the court poet asks the king to go home in the middle of the war and gives the besieged enemy's rest as a reason, so the mullai motif of the rainy-season return becomes, in praise poetry, a way of asking for a pause in the fighting.

links.note: 82 lines 12 and 13 praise wealth that does not lessen however much singers take and an army that does not lessen however much foes kill (கொளக்கொளக் குறையா, கொலக்கொலக் குறையா); 90 line 16 makes the same quality the ground of a likeness: like the sea, because taking does not diminish him (கொளக்குறை படாமையின் முந்நர்ண அனையை).
links.teaches: Read together, the two poems show the poet's own method of comparison: a quality he first states as a bare formula about wealth and army becomes, in the last poem of the decade, the stated reason why the king is like the sea, so the ground of the simile is set out before the simile is made.

links.note: 72 says the king's foes resolve without deliberating (சூழாது துணிதல்) and, from the greatness of their folly, do not know his nature as the wise do; 84 says his foes knew well that he was strong (வலியை ஆதல்நற்(கு) அறிந்தனர் ஆயினும்) and still rose against him, not knowing how to bow.
links.teaches: The two Chera decades give opposite causes for the same ruin: the eighth ten blames the enemy's ignorance of the king, the ninth blames their refusal to bow although they knew him, which moves the fault from a lack of judgement to pride.

links.note: In 61 Kapilar comes to the Chera after Pari's death, saying he will not beg or understate but has come for the king's fame for giving; 85 says this later Chera's gifts are more than the villages Kapilan won (கபிலன் பெற்ற ஊரினும் பலவே).
links.teaches: The seventh ten shows Kapilar arriving at the Chera court without a patron, and the ninth uses the reward he got there as the standard a later king's giving is said to exceed, so one poet's payment became the dynasty's own yardstick for generosity.

links.note: Purananuru 105 says Pari's gentleness is sweeter than the water that comes down every peak of his hill (நீரினும் இனிய சாயல்); Patitruppattu 86 says Poraiyan is sweeter and cooler of gentleness than the water of the Vaani (வானி நீரினும் தீந்தண் சாயலன்), after the poet admits he had feared him for his slaughter in war.
links.teaches: The formula of a patron gentler than running water passes from Kapilar's hill chief to a Chera king, but the later poet sets it against the king's reputation for bloodshed, so the same praise is used to answer a suppliant's fear of a warrior king.

links.note: Kural 386 says the land of a king easy to see and not harsh of speech is praised above others; Patitruppattu 86 tells how the report of the king's killing in war made the poet fear him, until he found him the patron of singers who ends the misery of the poor and is gentle as cool river water.
links.teaches: The couplet treats being easy to approach as a plain royal virtue, while the poem shows what it has to overcome: a king's fame for killing keeps suppliants away, so his accessibility has to be proved against his own reputation.

links.note: Purananuru 105 sends a bright-browed virali to Pari, saying she will get jewels (சேயிழை பெறுகுவை) and likening his gentleness to water coming down his hill; Patitruppattu 87 sends a singing woman to Poraiyan, saying she will get fine jewels (நன்கலம் பெறுகுவை) and setting his kindness against the cane carried by a flood that bears sandal to the sea.
links.teaches: Perunkunrur Kizhar splits Kapilar's single guide poem into two of his own, the water likeness in 86 and the sending of the singer with the promise of jewels in 87, which shows how a short Purananuru guide poem served the Patitruppattu poets as a pattern they could take apart.

links.note: The fourth preface tells Narmudi Cheral's own deed: he cut off Nannan's head and felled his gold-bearing vaakai at the root (பொன்படு வாகை முழுமுதல் தடிந்து); 88 lists the wearing down of Nannan of the bright-flowered vaakai (சுடர்வீ வாகை நன்னன் தேய்த்து) among the deeds of the ancestors (பெரியோர் மருக) of the ninth ten's king.
links.teaches: A victory that the fourth decade gives to one named king appears in the ninth as one item in a list of ancestral deeds, beside the kadamba and the spear thrown into the sea, so the decades show single kings' wars becoming the common record of the Chera line.

links.note: 20 answers 'who is your king?' with Neduncheralathan, who went against foes on an island of the sea and cut the kadamba at its root (கடம்புமுதல் தடிந்த); 88 has the kadamba's whole trunk felled and the spear hurled into the dark sea as deeds of the ancestors of the present king.
links.teaches: In the second ten the felling of the kadamba is what identifies one king to a stranger, and in the ninth it has become an inherited title that makes a later king great by descent, so the pair shows a personal feat hardening into a dynastic emblem.

links.note: Kural 545 says rain and harvest gather in the land of the king who rules by the right way; Patitruppattu 89 lists the rain in its season, the paired deer, the humming boughs, unfailing fruit and tubers, grazing herds and endless grain, then gives the cause: because your sceptre is straight (நின்கோல் செம்மையின்).
links.teaches: The couplet states the link between a just sceptre and rain as a rule, while the poem spreads its consequences over a whole countryside of herds, forest creatures and grain, which shows how wide a land's well-being the belief was taken to cover.

links.note: Purananuru 35 counsels the Chola that rain comes when sought in a land of the just sceptre and warns that if rain fails or yield shrinks the world blames its guardians (காவலர்ப் பழிக்கும்); Patitruppattu 89 tells the Chera that rain pours in season because his sceptre is straight and the land worships him daily.
links.teaches: The same belief works as praise in one poem and as warning in the other: credit for the rain in the Chera poem implies the blame for drought that the Chola poem spells out, so a king praised for good seasons was held answerable for bad ones.

links.note: Purananuru 2 says the Chera has forbearance, breadth of counsel, strength, fierceness and grace like the nature of the five elements, without saying which goes with which; Patitruppattu 90 likens the king to water for his kindness, to the sky for being beyond measure and to the sea for not lessening however much is taken, naming each ground.
links.teaches: The ninth ten does explicitly what the Purananuru catalogue leaves implicit, joining each natural power to one royal virtue by a stated reason, so the pair shows the elemental praise of Chera kings being turned from a list into reasoned comparison.

links.note: The seventh preface says Selvakkadungo, after his sacrifice, gave Ogandur and 'confounded the purohita' (புரோசு மயக்கி); the ninth preface uses the same phrase of Ilanjeral Irumporai (புரைஅறு கேள்விப் புரோசு மயக்கி), beside mantra worship, the installing of the spirits of the crossroads and the shanti rite.
links.teaches: The repeated phrase shows that the preface-writers had a fixed slot for a king's dealings with his purohita, and the ninth preface fills it with a larger ritual programme than the seventh, so the prefaces record the growing weight given to priestly rites in the picture of Chera kingship.

source_issues: 81-90: no poem colophon gives a thinai (all null); the patikam has neither thinai nor thurai.
88: the colophon thurai செந்துறைப்பாடாண்பாட்டு is written without spaces; normalised in puram_thurai names. 83's தும்பையரவம் is normalised as தும்பை அரவம்.
81 is marked mixed and mullai against a puram thurai முல்லை: the poem ends with the request that the king go home to his wife in the rains, which is the akam situation of mullai.
85 line 1 தாணஇப் looks like an unrepaired TSCII leftover (ணஇ for ரீஇ, as repaired at 90 line 23); not flagged.
90 line 16 முந்நர்ண is probably a misprint for முந்நீர்; 84 line 14 உடன்(ரு)எழுந்(து) is probably உடன்று எழுந்து; 81 line 4 விசும்(பு)அடையூ is odd.
82 line 12 has a comma inside the line (பாடுநர், கொளக்கொள); 90 line 51 likewise (நின்நாள், திங்கள்).
Repaired TSCII leftovers (flags) at 81 line 8, 86 line 12, 88 line 34 and 90 line 23; the repaired readings are plausible.
patikam:9 line 18 (பாடினார் பத்துப்பாட்டு.) is the prose colophon kept as a verse line.
